newsitem.title: CHINA: Academic freedom row flares in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Academic freedom row flares in Hong Kong.

text.p: A quarrel with a whiff of racism has flared up over academic freedom in Hong Kong just five weeks after China took over the former British colony.
A pro-China politician sparked the row when he wrote to universities to attack politically outspoken professors.

It is the latest in a series of polemics in the former British colony over basic freedoms, which Hong Kong liberals consider to be under threat now that communist-ruled China wields sovereignty over the capitalist enclave.

The public heard a ferocious exchange on a radio breakfast show on Tuesday when journalism professor Tim Hamlett of the Baptist University accused pro-China legislator and businessman David Chu of waging a racist campaign to drive out foreigners.

In another episode, Professor Richard Baum of the Chinese University of Hong Kong wrote in a letter published on Monday that Chu had written to his superiors demanding his sacking because he criticised Chu's nationalist education proposals.
Chu is campaigning to erase colonial influence from Hong Kong education. His speeches and newspaper columns have often expressed nationalistic views with a strong whiff of xenophobia.
Baum and Hamlett are among hundreds of foreign university teachers working in Hong Kong. Both academics have challenged Chu's views in newspaper letters and articles.

Chu wrote a letter to Baum's superiors suggesting he was unfit to be a guest in Hong Kong. He also sent a critical fax to Hamlett's superiors. "I think it's the rudest communication I've ever received," Hamlett told Chu in their live radio quarrel.
"You'd make a very good recruit for the National Front," he said, referring to a British neo-fascist group. "I've never read such racist abuse and festering frustrations," Hamlett said.
Chu said he "copied" the letter to Hamlett's bosses so they "would be kept abreast of what's happening".
Hamlett, a Briton, accused Chu of having a policy to attack people on the basis of nationality and writing surreptitiously to their employers. "That's a disgraceful policy," he said.
Hamlett challenged Chu to publish the letter to let the public see how abusive and rude he had been. He said Chu held "personal resentments of anyone who has a foreign surname".
In a newspaper article Hamlett had taken issue with Chu's charges that the Western media had spread doomsday scenarios about Hong Kong's prospects under Chinese sovereignty.
Chu would not say whether he had said Baum was unfit to teach and should leave Hong Kong. Baum, a noted China expert, is a visiting scholar financed by the University of California.
The Chinese University and Baptist University on Monday defended the right of their staff to criticise Chu's views, saying freedom of expression must be preserved.

Hong Kong University's law department has also been a centre of vocal criticism of the new government. Law dons have attacked the post-colonial rollback of civil liberties and democracy, and have challenged the constitutionality of new laws.
One law professor there claims he was not given a new contract because of his political statements.
In May, law professor Raymond Wacks called for a watchdog body to be set up to guard academic freedom after the handover on June 30.
At the Chinese University, students protested earlier this year against a plan to remove a foreign lecturer.
Hong Kong's City University meanwhile has circulated a note to faculty staff telling them to seek approval before giving interviews or publishing manuscripts.
A few months ago a rumpus at City University led to the ousting of two law professors who criticised declining English language standards.
The South China Morning Post said in an editorial Chu's letter to Baum's superiors had been interpreted "as an attempt to silence an unwelcome critic".
Hong Kong was a British colony for 156 years until July 1.
Its 6.4 million people are mostly Chinese. The foreign community numbers about 450,000, including about 32,000 Britons, far fewer than the 140,000 Filipinos and 37,200 Americans.
